Implementation fidelity: scholar plan + system

See full role expectations

Role-specific MTSS pathways

Everyone participates in MTSS, but not everyone owns the same decisions. These pathways clarify the work expected from common GRPS roles.

Principal / Building Leader

Owns the system.

Protect Tier 1 quality, establish meeting cadence, ensure intervention capacity, remove implementation barriers, monitor fidelity and outcomes, and prevent MTSS from becoming a referral-only process.

Classroom Teacher

Owns daily Tier 1 access and evidence.

Differentiate core instruction/supports, notice patterns, document classroom strategies and response, contribute precise evidence, implement assigned supports, and communicate with families.

MTSS Scholar Success Teacher

Owns targeted intervention delivery and monitoring.

Deliver supplemental academic/behavioral/SEL supports, maintain intervention documentation, progress monitor, coordinate with classroom staff and families, and surface fidelity or capacity concerns.

FSS / KSSN / Support Staff

Owns barrier removal and coordinated supports.

Identify nonacademic barriers, connect scholars/families to school and community resources, coordinate attendance and wellness plans, bring family voice to problem solving, and track whether the barrier is actually being reduced.

Detailed Tier 2 / Tier 3 decision guidance
TIER 2 / TIER 3 DECISION GUIDANCE

Entry, intensification, fading and exit

Tier labels should describe the intensity of support—not a destination or permanent placement.

DecisionEvidence to requireWhat the team does
Enter Tier 2Specific need/barrier is defined; Tier 1 access has been verified; data show the scholar needs supplemental support.Select a matched intervention with explicit dosage, owner, goal, progress measure and review date.
ContinueProgress trend is adequate and fidelity is strong.Continue through the planned duration; do not change a working intervention prematurely.
Adjust / IntensifyProgress is inadequate while fidelity is strong.Increase precision or intensity: smaller group, more time, increased frequency, stronger match, added component, or Tier 3 problem solving.
Repair FidelityProgress is inadequate and implementation is inconsistent.Fix scheduling, staffing, training, dosage or critical components before declaring the intervention ineffective.
Fade / ExitGoal is met and performance is stable/generalizing.Reduce supplemental support deliberately while continuing Tier 1 and monitoring maintenance.
Tier 3 / IntensiveNeed is significant, persistent, complex, or insufficiently responsive to well-implemented targeted support.Use individualized problem solving, increase intensity and monitoring frequency, coordinate multiple supports where needed, and document response.
Important: Tier 3 does not automatically mean special education, and special education is not a “Tier 4.” Evaluation decisions follow applicable legal criteria and comprehensive evidence, not a simple sequence of failed tiers.
TIER 1 SCHOOLWIDE ANALYSIS

Before individualizing, test the system

Use these three checks when the same concern appears across multiple scholars, classrooms, courses, or settings.

1 · Who is affected?Look for concentration by grade, course, classroom, subgroup, time, location, or setting.Review pattern →2 · Is Tier 1 accessible and implemented?Check instruction, universal supports, opportunity to learn, climate, schedule, staffing, and fidelity.Check implementation →3 · What system change is most likely to help?Change the environment, instruction, routine, or adult practice—then monitor implementation and outcomes.Build the response →
See the full schoolwide-analysis guidance

Tier 1 schoolwide analysis

Before individualizing, teams should test whether the pattern is actually a system problem.

1. Who is affected?

Disaggregate by grade, classroom/course, subgroup, time, location and setting. Look for concentration rather than relying on one aggregate rate.

2. Is Tier 1 accessible and implemented?

Check instructional/support expectations, schedule, opportunity to learn, climate, attendance conditions, staffing and fidelity.

3. What is the smallest system change likely to help?

Select a response that changes the environment, instruction, routine or adult practice—then measure implementation and outcomes.

Open the complete example

What an implementation-ready plan looks like

EXAMPLE · ATTENDANCE

Scholar misses first period 2–3 days each week

Need/barrier: Morning transportation is unreliable after a family schedule change. The primary issue is access—not motivation.

Evidence: 9 first-period absences in 20 school days; later periods are attended at 94%; scholar/family interview confirms transportation barrier.

Intervention: Family + FSS develop a reliable primary and backup transportation plan; designated adult checks arrival for 10 school days and troubleshoots missed connections the same day.

Owner / dosage: FSS coordinates plan; daily arrival check for 10 school days.

Progress measure: First-period attendance daily. Fidelity: transportation plan available and check completed each school day.

Decision rule: If first-period attendance reaches ≥90% for 10 consecutive school days, fade daily check to twice weekly. If attendance remains below 80% with full fidelity, reconvene to identify an additional or different barrier.

GRPS model

How MTSS Works in GRPS

GRPS organizes MTSS across four connected areas. Teams use the same problem-solving process across domains, while supports may differ in intensity depending on the scholar or system need.

Academics

High-quality core instruction, screening, differentiation, targeted intervention, progress monitoring, and intensification.

Attendance

Universal prevention, early identification, root-cause inquiry, barrier removal, engagement, and individualized attendance support.

Mental Health / SEL

Belonging, explicit SEL instruction, targeted supports, referral/coordination, and appropriate intensive or community-based services.

PBIS / Behavior

Schoolwide expectations, restorative and preventive practices, targeted behavior supports, and individualized problem solving.

Tier 1 — UniversalStrong core instruction and schoolwide supports for all scholars, with screening and differentiation.
Tier 2 — TargetedAdditional strategic support matched to a defined need while Tier 1 continues.
Tier 3 — IntensiveMore individualized and intensive support matched to a persistent need, while Tier 1 and applicable Tier 2 supports continue.
Ready to apply the model?Use the System Map to move from Tier 1 and problem definition to support, implementation, monitoring, and decision making.

See the full operating model and role details
GRPS operating model

Who Solves What?

Use the lowest level of the system that can effectively solve the problem. Move a need or system barrier upward when additional coordination, authority, resources, expertise, or system change is required—not simply because a scholar is struggling.

Level 1

Classroom / Grade / Content Team

  • Strengthens Tier 1 instruction, routines, relationships, and differentiation.
  • Notices patterns and defines concerns.
  • Uses readily available data and scholar/family information.
  • Implements reasonable classroom/team supports.
  • Identifies when coordinated problem solving is needed.
Level 2

Scholar Success Team

  • Solves defined scholar-level or small-group problems requiring coordination.
  • Clarifies root cause/need and matches intervention.
  • Coordinates academic and nonacademic supports.
  • Sets owner, dosage, monitoring, fidelity, review date, and decision rule.
  • Intensifies deliberately when evidence supports it.
Level 3

Building MTSS Leadership Team

  • Owns buildingwide MTSS implementation.
  • Reviews Tier 1 health and schoolwide/subgroup patterns.
  • Manages intervention capacity, schedules, staffing, and access.
  • Monitors whether SST and intervention systems are functioning.
  • Removes building-level implementation barriers.
Level 4

District MTSS Support

  • Establishes common framework, standards, tools, and expectations.
  • Builds school capacity through professional learning and coaching.
  • Reviews cross-school patterns and implementation data.
  • Allocates/aligns resources and removes district-level barriers.
  • Addresses issues requiring district authority or cross-department coordination.
Important: This is not a referral ladder. A need does not have to travel through every level. Building and district teams may act directly when data reveal a system-level problem.

Decision Rights & Evidence

LevelPrimary questionEvidence reviewedTypical decisionsMove / connect when…
Classroom / Grade / ContentWhat can we change in Tier 1 or routine support now?Classwork, common assessments, attendance, engagement/behavior, classroom implementation, scholar/family information.Reteach, differentiate, adjust routines/access, strengthen relationships, short-cycle support, monitor.The need persists, spans domains, requires coordinated intervention, or affects many scholars.
Scholar Success TeamWhat specifically is getting in the way, and what matched support will change it?Defined problem, root-cause evidence, Tier 1 context, prior supports, progress, fidelity/access, scholar/family voice.Initiate/modify targeted plan, coordinate partners, intensify, fade/exit, request system action.The barrier cannot be solved at scholar-team level or data reveal a broader system condition.
Building MTSS LeadershipIs our building system producing equitable access and adequate outcomes?Universal/benchmark data, attendance, discipline/behavior, belonging, subgroup patterns, intervention capacity, fidelity, SST trends.Strengthen Tier 1, redesign schedules/processes, allocate staff/time, set building priorities, request district support.The issue requires district resources, policy, cross-school coordination, technical assistance, or authority.
District MTSS SupportWhat district conditions will help schools implement MTSS consistently and effectively?Cross-school outcomes, implementation/fidelity patterns, resource/capacity data, equity patterns, building requests.Set standards, align resources, provide tools/PD/coaching, solve cross-department barriers, adjust district systems.Implementation evidence shows additional policy/resource/organizational action is needed.

Connect to another level when…

  • The team lacks authority or resources to remove the barrier.
  • The same pattern appears across multiple classrooms, grades, or schools.
  • Intervention capacity or scheduling prevents adequate implementation.
  • Multiple departments/services must coordinate.
  • Fidelity problems reflect a system condition rather than one case.

Do not escalate simply because…

  • A scholar scored below benchmark once.
  • A teacher wants another person to “take over.”
  • A parent contact or referral has already occurred.
  • The team has not yet defined the need.
  • The intervention was not implemented long enough or with adequate fidelity/access.

GRPS problem-solving process

From Need to Decision

The purpose of MTSS is not to move scholars through tiers. It is to solve a defined problem with the least intensive support likely to work, implement it well, and use evidence to decide what happens next.

NOTICEIdentify the pattern
UNDERSTANDDefine need + why
MATCHSelect support
PLANOwner + dosage + goal
IMPLEMENTDeliver as designed
MONITOROutcome + fidelity
DECIDEContinue / modify / intensify / fade
Guardrail: Do not wait for a formal meeting to begin reasonable Tier 1 supports or to remove an obvious access barrier. The meeting exists to improve problem solving and coordination—not to delay support.

Scholar Success Team

When the Scholar Success Team Adds Value

Use the Scholar Success Team when the need requires coordinated problem solving beyond routine classroom or grade-level support, when response is unclear, or when multiple domains or partners must be aligned.

Bring these six things

1. Clear need
Observable and measurable, not a label.
2. Current evidence
Outcome data plus relevant qualitative evidence.
3. Tier 1 context
What core supports and differentiation are already in place?
4. What has been tried
Include implementation details, not just a list of actions.
5. Scholar/family voice
What does the scholar or family say is helping or getting in the way?
6. Decision needed
What must the team decide today?

Every SST meeting should end with

  • A precise problem/root-cause statement.
  • A matched intervention or system action.
  • A named owner and partner roles.
  • Frequency/dosage, duration, and start date.
  • A progress-monitoring measure and fidelity check.
  • A review date and explicit decision rule.
If the team cannot name these items, the plan is not yet implementation-ready.
DATA USE

Review the right evidence at the right level

Match the evidence to the decision level so teams do not over-analyze individual cases or under-analyze system patterns.

Classroom / Grade / ContentUse immediate instructional evidence, scholar work, common assessments, attendance/behavior patterns, and implementation data.Classroom/team decisions →Scholar Success TeamUse baseline, problem definition, scholar/family voice, prior support, progress, and fidelity/access evidence.SST decisions →Building MTSS TeamUse aggregated outcomes, subgroup/context patterns, Tier 1 implementation, intervention capacity, and experience/access data.Building decisions →DistrictUse cross-school patterns, system barriers, resource/capacity needs, and implementation variation.District decisions →
See full data-level guidance
Data cadence

Review the Right Data at the Right Level

MTSS data review should distinguish schoolwide patterns from individual response. This prevents buildings from using scholar-level meetings to solve Tier 1 or organizational problems.

Universal / Benchmark Review

Typical cadence: Fall, winter, spring and after major benchmark windows.

Ask: Are enough scholars succeeding with Tier 1? Where are subgroup, grade, course, attendance, belonging, or behavior patterns concentrated?

Decision: Strengthen core/system conditions before creating unnecessary individual plans.

Targeted Support Review

Typical cadence: Regular grade/content/team review based on intervention cycle.

Ask: Is the support reaching the right scholars, delivered at the intended dosage, and producing the expected rate of progress?

Decision: Continue, correct fidelity, modify, intensify, or fade.

Intensive / Individual Review

Typical cadence: More frequent, based on need and intervention design.

Ask: What does the combined outcome + fidelity + access + experience evidence show?

Decision: Individualize or intensify deliberately; coordinate across domains and services as needed.

See detailed assessment guidance
Assessment system

Use Assessment to Answer a Question

Assessment is useful only when the team is clear about the decision it needs to make. GRPS teams should use the smallest amount of evidence necessary to answer the question reliably.

Universal screening

Purpose: Identify schoolwide strengths, needs, and scholars who may require additional support.

Use for: Tier 1 evaluation, early identification, subgroup analysis, and intervention capacity planning.

Do not use for: Making a complete diagnosis from one score.

Diagnostic / root-cause evidence

Purpose: Understand the specific skill gap, barrier, function, or condition contributing to the defined need.

Use for: Selecting or adapting an intervention.

Do not use for: Delaying support while teams collect unnecessary data.

Progress monitoring

Purpose: Determine whether the scholar is responding to the intervention at the expected rate.

Use for: Continue, change, intensify, or fade decisions.

Do not use for: Monitoring unrelated outcomes that do not reflect the target skill or barrier.

Fidelity / implementation evidence

Purpose: Verify that the support was actually delivered as designed.

Use for: Interpreting outcome data and identifying implementation barriers.

Do not use for: Punitive evaluation of individual staff.

Decision rule: Never conclude that an intervention “did not work” until the team can reasonably verify adequate access, sufficient time, and acceptable implementation fidelity.
Screen for strengths and needsUniversal screening should help teams identify schoolwide strengths, needs, and scholars who may require additional support.
Match the measure to the questionDo not collect more data than the decision requires. Diagnostic and progress measures should align directly to the defined need.
Plan progress monitoring before implementationName the measure, goal, collection frequency, owner, fidelity evidence, and review rule before the intervention cycle begins.

Intervention planning

The GRPS Intervention Plan Standard

A strong plan is specific enough that another trained staff member could understand what is supposed to happen, who is responsible, and how the team will know whether it worked.

Define the need. State the academic skill, attendance barrier, behavioral function/pattern, or SEL/mental-health-related need precisely.
State the goal. Define the measurable change expected by the review date.
Name the intervention. Identify the support and explain why it matches the need.
Define dosage. Frequency, minutes, group size, setting, and duration.
Name the owner. One lead person is accountable for ensuring implementation occurs; partners may share tasks.
Define the progress measure. Specify what evidence will show scholar response.
Define the fidelity measure. Identify how the team will verify implementation.
Set the review date. Choose a date aligned to the intervention cycle—not an arbitrary calendar date.
Set the decision rule. State in advance what evidence will trigger continue, change, intensify, fade, or exit.
⌂ MTSS HomeSystem Map →
Family partnership

Families Are Partners in Problem Solving

Family engagement should improve the team's understanding of the scholar's strengths, experience, barriers, and response to support. It should not be reduced to notifying families after decisions have already been made.

Before the plan

  • Share the identified need or pattern in clear, nontechnical language.
  • Ask what the family and scholar are noticing.
  • Identify strengths, successful routines, cultural/linguistic considerations, and barriers.
  • Clarify what the school is already doing at Tier 1.

During implementation

  • Explain the intervention, goal, owner, and review date.
  • Agree on the most useful communication method and frequency.
  • Avoid repeated requests for the family to retell the same story to multiple staff.
  • Ask whether the support is improving the scholar's actual experience.

At review

  • Share progress and fidelity evidence.
  • Ask whether the original barrier or need has changed.
  • Discuss continue / modify / intensify / fade decisions before finalizing them.
  • Document new responsibilities and next review point.

Communication standard

Communication should be understandable, respectful, culturally responsive, and available in the family's preferred language when needed.

A family contact is not automatically an intervention. It becomes part of an intervention only when it contributes directly to changing the identified barrier or condition.

Ready to incorporate voice?Carry scholar/family strengths, barriers, and priorities into the problem definition and plan.

Implementation fidelity

Check Implementation Before Changing the Plan

Fidelity questionWhat the team should verifyIf weak
Was the intervention delivered?Sessions/supports actually occurred as planned.Repair scheduling, staffing, or access before judging effectiveness.
Was the intended dosage reached?Minutes, frequency, group size, and duration were adequate.Correct dosage before intensifying content unnecessarily.
Was the intervention delivered as designed?Critical components and instructional/support routines were present.Provide coaching, modeling, or implementation support.
Did the scholar have access?Attendance, scheduling, transportation, behavior, or other barriers did not prevent participation.Remove the access barrier and re-establish adequate exposure.
Was progress measured as planned?Enough valid data points exist to interpret response.Collect the missing evidence before making a major decision.
Implementation verified?Use the intensification guidance only after confirming adequate delivery and access.

Documentation

Document the Decision, Not Just the Activity

Useful MTSS documentation should allow another team member to understand what problem was identified, what support was selected, whether it happened, what changed, and what decision was made.

Minimum case record

  • Need/problem statement
  • Root-cause or need hypothesis
  • Intervention and rationale
  • Owner + partners
  • Start date + dosage + duration
  • Progress measure + fidelity measure
  • Review date
  • Decision + next step

Avoid documentation overload

  • Do not duplicate the same plan across multiple tools unless required.
  • Do not document every contact as if it were a separate intervention.
  • Do not collect information the team will not use to make a decision.
  • Keep protected information limited to what is necessary for the educational purpose.

Examples

What Implementation-Ready MTSS Looks Like

Defined needWeak responseImplementation-ready response
Scholar is chronically absent. Send attendance letter and refer to FSS. Family/scholar inquiry identifies unreliable transportation. FSS coordinates a reliable morning transportation plan for 20 school days; team monitors successful rides + weekly attendance and reviews after four weeks.
Scholar is significantly below reading benchmark. Place in reading intervention. Diagnostic evidence identifies decoding as the primary gap. Scholar receives explicit decoding intervention 4×30 minutes/week in a group of 4 for 6 weeks; weekly decoding probe + fidelity check guide continue/intensify decision.
Repeated disruption occurs during independent work. Behavior referral and parent phone call. Team defines the pattern, checks classroom routines, and identifies task avoidance linked to skill difficulty. Teacher adjusts task access and teaches a help-seeking routine; progress is monitored through work completion + observed use of replacement behavior.
Many scholars in one grade are struggling. Refer multiple scholars to Tier 2. Grade team reviews core instruction, common assessment patterns, opportunity to learn, and implementation fidelity. Team strengthens Tier 1 before determining which scholars still require supplemental support.

Working tools

Complete the MTSS Work Here

These tools convert the Field Manual from guidance into an operating resource. They are intentionally concise so teams can use them during actual planning and review meetings.

Intervention Plan Builder

Build an implementation-ready plan in six short decisions. The tool keeps the technical fields in the background and shows one decision at a time.

No intervention selected yet.
Choose a support from the Matched-Support Library or Academic Support Finder, or build a plan from scratch.
← Choose supportAcademic finderSee examples
Step 1 of 6

What are we trying to change?

Define the need precisely enough that another staff member could recognize it. Avoid labels such as “struggling,” “unmotivated,” or “poor attendance” without describing the actual pattern.

Step 2 of 6

What will we do—and why does it match?

Name the actual intervention/support, not an action such as “call home,” “refer to SST,” or “check in.” Explain how it addresses the defined need or barrier.

Intervention check: If the entry only describes something staff did—sent a letter, made a call, held a meeting, made a referral—it is probably an action, not the intervention itself.
Step 3 of 6

Who owns implementation?

Assign one lead owner. Partners may support the work, but shared ownership without a lead usually creates implementation drift.

Example: “Ms. Rivera — lead; classroom teacher and FSS — partners.”
Step 4 of 6

What will implementation actually look like?

Specify frequency, duration, group size/setting when relevant, and expected length of the first implementation cycle.

Step 5 of 6

How will we know whether it is working?

Track both the scholar outcome and whether the support was actually delivered/accessed as intended.

Do not intensify from outcome data alone. First confirm that the support was delivered with sufficient dosage and the scholar had meaningful access/exposure.
Step 6 of 6

When will we review—and what will the evidence mean?

Set the review date now. Then define the decision rule before seeing the next data so the team is not changing expectations after the fact.

Complete the six decisions to create an implementation-ready summary.

SST Decision Record

Use this record to document the decision—not a transcript of the meeting.

Tier 1 Health Check

Complete the four checks before referring large numbers of scholars for supplemental intervention.
Tier 1 benchmark note: A percentage such as 80% can be a useful system-health heuristic, but it should not function as a rigid referral cutoff. Use GRPS-adopted outcome expectations, subgroup patterns, fidelity, access, and context together.

The monitoring measure should align directly with the intervention target.

Show me

See What Strong MTSS Work Looks Like

Use these examples to calibrate team expectations. They are examples of structure and reasoning—not scripts that should be copied without matching the actual need.

Example: Attendance Barrier-Removal Plan

Concern
Scholar attended 74% of the last 20 instructional days.
Evidence
Four of five recent absences occurred when the family's usual transportation was unavailable; family interview confirms transportation instability.
Intervention
Establish reliable morning transportation plus a backup plan for 20 instructional days.
Owner
FSS coordinates the plan; family confirms changes; school attendance contact reviews successful access weekly.
Monitor
Days present, planned rides completed, and family report that the transportation barrier is decreasing.
Decision
Continue/fade when access is stable and attendance improves; modify if rides are not occurring; investigate other causes if access is stable but attendance remains low.

Example: Tier 2 Reading Plan

Need
Diagnostic evidence indicates a decoding deficit rather than a general “low reading” concern.
Goal
Meet the established decoding progress target by the six-week review.
Intervention
Evidence-based explicit decoding intervention aligned to the identified skill need.
Dosage
4 × 30 minutes/week, group of four, for six weeks.
Monitor
Weekly skill-aligned progress monitoring plus intervention attendance and fidelity.
Decision
Continue if response is adequate; repair fidelity/access first when weak; intensify deliberately when adequate fidelity/access and data show inadequate response.

Example: Strong SST Decision

Problem
Scholar completes fewer than 30% of independent mathematics tasks requiring multi-step computation.
Hypothesis
Work samples and brief diagnostic evidence indicate prerequisite computation gaps; disruption occurs primarily after difficult tasks are assigned.
Decision
Provide targeted prerequisite-skill instruction while adjusting independent-task entry points and explicitly teaching a help-seeking routine.
Ownership
Interventionist provides skill support; teacher implements task/access adjustments and help-seeking routine.
Evidence
Skill probe, task completion, replacement behavior, intervention exposure, fidelity.
Review
Team reviews at the end of the defined intervention cycle using the pre-established decision rule.

Example: Deliberate Intensification

Before changing
Team confirms sufficient intervention time, acceptable fidelity, adequate attendance/access, and enough progress data to identify a trend.
Finding
Scholar is not on track to meet the goal despite adequate implementation.
Adaptation
Increase opportunities to respond and feedback, reduce group size, and strengthen explicitness while keeping the validated intervention platform aligned to the same need.
Monitoring
Add a phase line/start date; continue aligned progress monitoring and verify fidelity to the intensified plan.
Decision
Review response to the adaptation rather than changing multiple variables at once.

Example: Tier 1 System Response

Pattern
A large share of Grade 6 scholars are failing the same mathematics standard.
Wrong move
Create dozens of Tier 2 referrals.
System inquiry
Review common assessment items, instructional opportunity, pacing, prerequisite skill demands, classroom implementation, and subgroup patterns.
Response
Strengthen/reteach the core instructional sequence and monitor classwide response.
Then
Identify scholars who remain below expectation after the Tier 1 response and determine whether supplemental support is warranted.
GRADE-BAND GUIDANCE

MTSS changes by developmental and instructional context

Select the grade span to focus the questions, supports, and progress evidence that make sense for that setting.

PK–5Emphasize foundational academics, early attendance patterns, routines, family partnership, and frequent skill-based progress evidence.Explore PK–5 supports →6–8Emphasize transition, course/period patterns, belonging, engagement, foundational skill gaps, and coordinated supports.Explore 6–8 pathway →9–12Emphasize credits, course performance, attendance by period, graduation trajectory, postsecondary relevance, and re-engagement.Explore 9–12 pathway →
See full grade-band guidance
Grade-band application

MTSS Looks Different Across Grade Spans

PK–5

Emphasize foundational literacy/numeracy, classroom behavior/SEL routines, attendance habits, family partnership, early screening, and rapid skill-specific support. Progress monitoring should align tightly to the taught skill.

6–8

Add course performance, transition to multiple teachers/settings, belonging, engagement, attendance patterns, behavior across settings, and early-warning indicators. Coordinate supports so scholars are not overloaded with disconnected interventions.

9–12

Use attendance, course failures, credits/on-track status, behavior, engagement/belonging, graduation trajectory, and EWIMS-style early warning. Intervention plans should account for schedule, credit recovery/acceleration, postsecondary relevance, and scholar voice.

Secondary guardrail: A scholar can be “on track” in one indicator and at significant risk in another. Teams should examine patterns across attendance, behavior/engagement, and course/credit performance rather than relying on a single threshold.

GRPS academic MTSS

Start With Grade-Level Core. Add Intensity With Purpose.

The GRPS academic guidance describes Tier 1 as the grade-level core provided to all scholars, with Tier 2 supplemental to and aligned with Tier 1. Tier 3 provides greater intensity and remains aligned to Tier 1 and Tier 2. The source notes that intensity may change through conditions such as time, focus, frequency/duration, and group size.

Do not confuse a resource with an intervention. A curriculum feature, digital program, scaffold, differentiation strategy, or technology tool becomes an MTSS intervention only when the team defines the target need, implementation conditions/dosage, owner, progress measure, fidelity/access evidence, review date, and decision rule.

Academic Support Finder

Answer four short questions. The finder will show the strongest matching GRPS options first; the full inventory stays in the background.

1 · Content→ 2 · Grade→ 3 · Level of need→ 4 · Skill / need

What content area needs support?

Choose the primary area. Start with the clearest instructional need.

What grade band?

This narrows the finder to resources aligned to the scholar's instructional context.

Which statement best describes the need?

Do not select intensity only because a scholar is behind. Use the evidence and implementation history.

What skill or need are you trying to address?

Use a short phrase such as phonemic awareness, fractions, vocabulary, or course access. You can also leave this blank to see all matches.

Advanced filter
No exact matches were found. Try a broader skill phrase, remove the advanced filter, or confirm that the content area and grade band are correct.

Tier 1 Academic Health: GRPS Essential Ingredients

Before creating large numbers of supplemental plans, examine whether rigorous grade-level instruction is consistently present. The academic guidance identifies seven GRPS essential ingredients:

Culturally affirming instruction
Standards-aligned learning targets unpacked, shared, and assessed with scholars
Scholar artifacts that illustrate modeling of thinking and ongoing learning
Classroom routines, norms, and expectations
Gradual release of responsibility: I do, we do, you do
Timely checking for understanding
Scholar talk/discourse, norms, and expectations
Tier 1 decision rule: When a pattern affects many scholars, first test whether core instruction, opportunity/access, implementation, or learning conditions need strengthening. Do not convert a Tier 1 problem into dozens of individual Tier 2 referrals.
Found a support?Move the selected support into the Plan Builder and define ownership, dosage, evidence, and review date.

GRPS support network

Match the Role to the Barrier

GRPS already has school and district roles that can strengthen MTSS implementation. The key is to use them as coordinated partners around a defined need—not as destinations for generic referrals.

Scholar Success

Scholar Success Coordinators and related school-based roles can help coordinate building-level scholar support, intervention follow-through, and cross-role problem solving where assigned.

KSSN / Community School

KSSN Coordinators can strengthen school-community connections and help coordinate resources around family/community barriers in participating schools.

GRPS KSSN team ↗

Family Support / Family Engagement

Use family-support and engagement capacity to listen, identify barriers, connect resources, strengthen family-school partnership, and verify whether the barrier was actually reduced.

Parent University ↗

SEL / Restorative Practices

GRPS SEL resources support universal and targeted skill development, relationships, restorative practices, coping, and family SEL resources.

GRPS SEL ↗

Mental Health / Qualified Supports

School mental-health clinicians and qualified community providers should be integrated when the defined need requires expertise beyond universal SEL or routine school supports.

Community & Student Services

The district's Community & Student Services mission explicitly includes linking home, school, and community and removing barriers that impede scholar growth and success.

Community & Student Services ↗
Actions vs. interventions: A phone call, referral, resource list, meeting, letter, or handoff documents something staff did. It becomes part of an intervention only when it is intentionally connected to changing the identified skill, barrier, behavior, or system condition and the team monitors whether that change occurred.

Looking for academic supports? Use the GRPS Academic Support Finder for the full content-area and grade-band menu.

This library is organized around the barrier or need to be solved, not around referrals or program names. Answer three short questions to see the most relevant supports first, then move the selected support into the Plan Builder.

1 · Area→ 2 · Barrier / need→ 3 · Scope

What is the primary area of need?

Start with the need that is most directly limiting access, participation, or success.

What seems to be getting in the way?

Choose the closest barrier or need. This is not a diagnosis; it helps match the next support.

How broad is the need or pattern?

This helps determine whether the first move should focus on the core system, a targeted group, or an individual plan.

GRPS guardrail: an action such as sending a letter or making a phone call documents activity; it is not itself an intervention. The intervention should intentionally remove the barrier, change the condition, or address the identified root cause.
No exact match was found. Broaden the barrier/need selection or use Multiple / Cross-domain to review coordinated options.

IMPLEMENTATION LIBRARY

GRPS Implementation Library

Use this section when the question is not “What is MTSS?” but “What should we do next?” Each pathway identifies the minimum evidence, implementation standard, monitoring expectation, and decision point.

Academic Support

Tier 1Tier 2Tier 3

Use when: screening, classroom performance, or progress-monitoring evidence indicates a defined skill need.

Do not use: a generic “low grades” label as the intervention target. Specify the skill or access barrier first.

Minimum plan: skill target, evidence-based practice/program, group size, frequency, duration, progress measure, fidelity check, review date.

Attendance & Engagement

Barrier-basedFamily partnership

Use when: attendance patterns show a barrier that can be matched to a support.

Do not use: calls, letters, conferences, or referrals as the intervention itself. Those are actions unless they directly remove the barrier or change the condition.

Minimum plan: barrier hypothesis, matched intervention, partner/owner, start date, frequency, attendance indicator, experience measure, review date.

Behavior / SEL / Mental Health

Function/need matchedProgress monitored

Use when: data identify a behavioral, social-emotional, belonging, regulation, or mental-health-related need.

Do not use: “behavior problem” as a sufficient problem statement. Define the observable pattern and context.

Minimum plan: operational need, prevention/teaching/support strategy, responsible adult, dosage, progress measure, fidelity check, family voice when appropriate.

GRPS decision guardrail: Additional tiers supplement strong Tier 1. A scholar may receive different levels of support in different domains at the same time. Tier 3 is not synonymous with special education.

Decision support

Should We Intensify the Intervention?

Use this quick check before increasing intensity. The intent is to prevent teams from changing interventions prematurely or intensifying when the real issue is implementation, access, or insufficient data.

Complete the four checks above.
If the evidence shows…Primary team responseWhat to document
Insufficient dataContinue the current plan long enough to obtain interpretable evidence.Next data point/date and review date.
Weak/uncertain fidelityRepair implementation before concluding the intervention is ineffective.Fidelity gap, coaching/support, follow-up check.
Weak access/attendanceAddress the access barrier; do not interpret low exposure as intervention failure.Barrier, barrier-removal intervention, exposure target.
Adequate data + fidelity + access + inadequate responseUse diagnostic information to intensify one or two dimensions deliberately.Adaptation, rationale, phase/start date, new fidelity check, review date.
Adequate responseContinue, fade, or exit according to the established decision rule.Response evidence and transition/maintenance plan.
Decision made?Update the plan, owner, dosage, progress evidence, and review date before leaving the meeting.

Meeting quality

Every MTSS Meeting Must Produce a Decision

A meeting is a coordination mechanism—not the intervention. Use this standard to prevent meetings that end with more discussion but no executable plan.

Required outputMinimum standardWeak exampleStrong example
Problem statementObservable, measurable, contextualized“Attendance issue”“Absent 6 of the last 20 days; 5 absences occurred on days transportation was unavailable.”
Root-cause hypothesisSupported by more than one source when feasible“Family doesn't value school”“Transportation instability is the primary barrier; family interview and absence pattern align.”
InterventionDesigned to change/remove the identified barrier or teach the needed skill“Call home weekly”“Establish reliable morning transportation for 4 weeks; FSS coordinates provider and confirms ride plan weekly.”
ImplementationOwner + frequency/dosage + start date + duration“Team will support”“FSS owns coordination; daily transportation support begins Sept. 8 for 20 instructional days.”
Progress measureDirectly related to intended change“Check in later”“Weekly days present and percent of planned rides successfully completed.”
Decision ruleDefines continue/change/intensify/fade“See how it goes”“At 4 weeks: continue if attendance improves and barrier is decreasing; revise if fidelity/access is weak; intensify if implemented as planned with inadequate response.”

Resource quality control

Before Adding a Resource to the Field Manual

1. Purpose

What specific MTSS task does this resource help a user complete?

2. Audience

Who should use it: leader, teacher, interventionist, support staff, scholar, or family?

3. Domain + Tier

Tag by Academics, Attendance, Behavior/PBIS, SEL/Mental Health and applicable tier(s).

4. Evidence / Authority

Prefer GRPS-approved, MDE/MiMTSS, or otherwise vetted evidence-based resources.

5. Usability

Users should know when to use it, how to use it, and what output it should produce.

6. Maintenance

Assign an owner and review date so the Field Manual does not become a graveyard of outdated links.

Design principle: the homepage should remain simple even as the manual becomes more powerful. Depth belongs behind task-based pathways, not on the first screen.
